**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics or computer science who knows maximum likelihood and has trained a classifier, and who wants models that say how much they do not know, and decisions that use it.

**Empirical first**: fit polynomials of degree 0 to 9 to 20 noisy points of a sine curve. The training error falls from 0.73 to 0.17 as the degree grows, so it cannot choose the degree. The Bayesian marginal likelihood of the same models, computed in closed form from the training data alone, peaks at degree 3 ([ch. 3](#ch3)). 

Five neural networks trained on 60 points agree to within 0.02 inside the data and spread to 0.24 far outside it, where all five miss the truth by about 3 ([ch. 8](#ch8)). Averaging models helps, but it is not yet a calibrated posterior.

This course treats Bayesian inference as a way of deciding under uncertainty. Choose the loss that matters, put a probability distribution on everything unknown, condition on the data, and act to minimize the posterior expected loss. The course then asks where priors come from, how to compute posteriors at the scale of machine learning, how to put priors on infinite-dimensional objects, and what survives of all this in deep learning.

It continues [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) and [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html), and shares tools with [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) and [Learning Physical Phenomena: Metamodelling and Uncertainty Quantification](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Formulate a learning task as a statistical decision problem and derive its Bayes rule for a given loss.
-   Compare decision rules by frequentist risk, Bayes risk, admissibility and minimaxity, and explain the James–Stein phenomenon.
-   Choose and defend a prior: exchangeability and elicitation, conjugate priors, Jeffreys and reference priors, empirical Bayes.
-   Check the frequentist behaviour of a Bayesian procedure with the Bernstein–von Mises theorem and coverage simulations.
-   Compute posterior and predictive distributions for Bayesian linear and logistic regression and for Gaussian processes, and select models by their marginal likelihood.
-   Build and sample Bayesian latent-variable models: mixtures, probabilistic PCA, topic models.
-   Implement and diagnose Metropolis–Hastings, Gibbs, Langevin, Hamiltonian and sequential Monte Carlo samplers.
-   Derive mean-field, stochastic and black-box variational approximations, and say what they get wrong.
-   Use the Dirichlet process and its mixtures, and state what posterior consistency and contraction rates mean.
-   Apply Laplace, variational, dropout, stochastic-gradient MCMC and ensemble approximations to neural networks, and evaluate them with proper scoring rules and calibration.
-   Read the abstract of a Bayesian machine learning paper, place it on the map of this course, and find a weak point worth a student seminar.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com states that by the end of the course students should have a high-level view of the main approaches to making decisions under uncertainty, and be able to detect when being Bayesian helps and why. They should be able to design and run a Bayesian machine learning pipeline for standard supervised or unsupervised learning.

They should also have a global view of the current limitations of Bayesian approaches and of the research landscape, and be able to understand the abstract of most Bayesian machine learning papers.

The description lists six themes. It announces 8 × 3 hours of lectures and practical sessions, in Python and R, and 4 hours of student seminars for the evaluation. The Université Paris-Saclay course detail gives the volume (16 h of lectures, 12 h of labs) and the type of assessment, with no programme of its own.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: an undergraduate course in probability, and a basic knowledge of Python and R. The description recommends the semester-1 course of P. Latouche and N. Chopin on probabilistic graphical models or that of S. Allassonière on computational statistics. Ch. 0 reviews the probability used throughout.

-   **Refreshers** — [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (conditional laws, Gaussian vectors, Markov chains), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (Schur complements, Hessians) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (the code).
-   **Semester 1 courses that prepare it** — [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) and [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html), the two recommended courses, give the first encounter with EM, mixtures, MCMC and variational methods. [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) treats the Langevin diffusions behind ch. 5 and ch. 8. [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) and [Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning](../s1-theoretical-foundations-dl/index.html) prepare ch. 8.
-   **Related courses of semester 2** — [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (the Gaussian-process posterior mean of ch. 3 is kernel ridge regression), [Learning Physical Phenomena](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html) (uncertainty quantification), [Inverse Problems and Imaging: Statistical and Stochastic Approaches](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html) and [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in Artificial Intelligence](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html) (posterior sampling with Langevin dynamics), [Sequential Learning](../s2-sequential-learning/index.html) (online decisions under uncertainty) and [Responsible Machine Learning](../s2-responsible-ml/index.html).
-   **Afterwards** — the [research internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html): the paper-study format of the evaluation is a rehearsal for it.

### Course outline

-   **0. Review** — Bayes' formula, Gaussian conditioning, exponential families and conjugacy, the Kullback–Leibler divergence, Markov chains.
-   **1. Decision theory** — losses and risks, Bayes rules, admissibility and minimaxity, complete classes, Stein's paradox, cost-sensitive classification.
-   **2. Fifty shades of Bayes** — subjective foundations (coherence, exchangeability), conjugate and objective priors, empirical Bayes, Bernstein–von Mises, the likelihood principle.
-   **3. Bayesian supervised learning** — linear regression, marginal likelihood, the Laplace approximation, logistic regression, Gaussian processes.
-   **4. Bayesian unsupervised learning** — mixtures and the Gibbs sampler, label switching, probabilistic PCA, topic models.
-   **5. Advanced Monte Carlo** — importance sampling, Metropolis–Hastings, Langevin and Hamiltonian samplers, diagnostics, sequential Monte Carlo.
-   **6. Variational methods** — the ELBO, mean field and coordinate ascent, stochastic and black-box VI, what the reverse KL misses.
-   **7. Bayesian nonparametrics** — the Dirichlet process, its urn and stick-breaking representations, DP mixtures, consistency and rates.
-   **8. Bayesian deep learning** — priors on weights, the Gaussian-process limit, Laplace, VI, dropout, SG-MCMC and ensembles, calibration, cold posteriors.
-   **9. Complements for self-study** — posterior consistency and contraction rates, the number of clusters, the Pitman–Yor urn, expectation propagation, the accuracy of variational Bayes.
-   **10. Research directions and open problems** — a self-study tour of current work, and how to read a paper.

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before session 1 if Gaussian conditioning or Markov chains feel distant; every later chapter uses them without warning.
-   After each session, do the exercises listed in its row, then run the code of the chapter and change one ingredient (the prior, the step size, the number of samples) to see its effect.
-   Write each sampler yourself once (Gibbs, Metropolis–Hastings, HMC, collapsed Gibbs for the DP mixture) before using a probabilistic programming language; each one is a few lines of NumPy.
-   The code uses NumPy, SciPy and PyTorch (CPU) with synthetic data; every block runs in under 30 seconds on a laptop.
-   Read ch. 9 after session 7 if you want the theory behind nonparametric posteriors and variational approximations.
-   Choose the paper for the seminar after session 5, and use ch. 10 to place it in the landscape.

## 0. Review: probability tools for Bayesian inference {#ch0}

Bayesian machine learning manipulates joint, marginal and conditional distributions, Gaussian vectors, exponential families, the Kullback–Leibler divergence and Markov chains. This chapter states the M1-level facts used later. The [Probability and Statistics refresher](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) covers the same ground at a slower pace.

### Bayes' formula for densities

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Bayesian model, posterior, predictive]{.tag} A **Bayesian model** consists of a family of densities $p(x \mid \theta)$ of the data, the **likelihood**, and a density $p(\theta)$ on the parameter, the **prior**. Densities are taken with respect to Lebesgue or counting measures. The **posterior** is the conditional density of $\theta$ given the data:
$$
p(\theta \mid x) = \frac{p(x \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)}{p(x)}, \qquad p(x) = \int p(x \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)\, d\theta .
$$

The normalizing constant $p(x)$ is the **marginal likelihood**, or **evidence**. If a new observation $x^\star$ is independent of $x$ given $\theta$, its **posterior predictive** density is
$$
p(x^\star \mid x) = \int p(x^\star \mid \theta)\, p(\theta \mid x)\, d\theta .
$$
:::

Two remarks are used constantly. First, the posterior is known up to a constant as soon as the product of likelihood and prior is, and the constant $p(x)$ is usually the hard part. Second, for independent observations the posterior can be updated one observation at a time: yesterday's posterior is today's prior.

### Gaussian vectors

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Conditioning a Gaussian vector]{.tag} Let $(u, v)$ be a Gaussian vector with means $\mu_u, \mu_v$ and covariance blocks $\Sigma_{uu}, \Sigma_{uv}, \Sigma_{vv}$, with $\Sigma_{vv}$ invertible. Then $u$ given $v$ is Gaussian:
$$
u \mid v \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_u + \Sigma_{uv} \Sigma_{vv}^{-1} (v - \mu_v),\;\; \Sigma_{uu} - \Sigma_{uv} \Sigma_{vv}^{-1} \Sigma_{vu}\big).
$$

::: proof
Set $A = \Sigma_{uv}\Sigma_{vv}^{-1}$ and $r = u - \mu_u - A(v - \mu_v)$.

-   The vector $(r, v)$ is Gaussian and $\mathrm{Cov}(r, v) = \Sigma_{uv} - A \Sigma_{vv} = 0$, so $r$ is independent of $v$.
-   Hence, given $v$, the vector $u = \mu_u + A(v - \mu_v) + r$ is Gaussian with the announced mean and covariance
    $$
    \mathrm{Cov}(r) = \Sigma_{uu} - A\Sigma_{vu} - \Sigma_{uv}A^\top + A\Sigma_{vv}A^\top = \Sigma_{uu} - \Sigma_{uv}\Sigma_{vv}^{-1}\Sigma_{vu} .
    $$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — The linear Gaussian model]{.tag} Let $\theta \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, S_0)$ and $y \mid \theta \sim \mathcal{N}(\Phi\theta, \Sigma)$. Then the marginal of $y$ and the posterior of $\theta$ are Gaussian:
$$
y \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\Phi m_0,\; \Sigma + \Phi S_0 \Phi^\top\big), \qquad \theta \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(m_N, S_N),
$$
$$
S_N^{-1} = S_0^{-1} + \Phi^\top \Sigma^{-1} \Phi, \qquad m_N = S_N\big(S_0^{-1} m_0 + \Phi^\top \Sigma^{-1} y\big).
$$

::: proof
Write $y = \Phi\theta + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ independent of $\theta$: the pair $(\theta, y)$ is Gaussian, which gives the marginal.

For the posterior, the logarithm of $p(y \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$ is, as a function of $\theta$,
$$
-\tfrac12\, \theta^\top \big(S_0^{-1} + \Phi^\top\Sigma^{-1}\Phi\big)\theta + \theta^\top\big(S_0^{-1}m_0 + \Phi^\top\Sigma^{-1}y\big) + \text{const},
$$
which is the logarithm of the announced Gaussian density up to a constant: complete the square. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### Exponential families and conjugacy

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Exponential family]{.tag} A family of densities is an **exponential family** with natural parameter $\eta$ and sufficient statistic $T$ if
$$
p(x \mid \eta) = h(x) \exp\big(\eta^\top T(x) - A(\eta)\big),
$$
where the log-partition function $A(\eta)$ normalizes the density. Differentiating under the integral gives $\nabla A(\eta) = \mathbb{E}_\eta[T(x)]$ and $\nabla^2 A(\eta) = \mathrm{Cov}_\eta[T(x)]$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Conjugate priors]{.tag} For $n$ independent observations from the family of Definition 0.4, the priors
$$
p(\eta \mid \nu, \tau) \propto \exp\big(\eta^\top \tau - \nu A(\eta)\big)
$$
form a **conjugate** family: the posterior belongs to it, with updated parameters
$$
\tau_n = \tau + \sum_{i=1}^n T(x_i), \qquad \nu_n = \nu + n .
$$

::: proof
The product of the prior and the $n$ likelihood factors is proportional to
$$
\exp\Big(\eta^\top\big(\tau + \textstyle\sum_i T(x_i)\big) - (\nu + n) A(\eta)\Big).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

The prior behaves like $\nu$ pseudo-observations with total sufficient statistic $\tau$. Ch. 2 uses this reading to elicit priors.
::::

::: ex
[Example 0.6 — Three conjugate pairs]{.tag}

-   Bernoulli likelihood and Beta$(a, b)$ prior: after $k$ successes in $n$ trials the posterior is Beta$(a + k, b + n - k)$. With a uniform prior and 7 successes in 10 trials, the posterior is Beta$(8, 4)$, with mean
    $$
    8/12 = 0.667 .
    $$
-   Poisson likelihood and Gamma$(a, b)$ prior (shape $a$, rate $b$): the posterior is Gamma$(a + \sum_i x_i,\; b + n)$.
-   Gaussian likelihood with known variance $\sigma^2$ and a $\mathcal{N}(m_0, s_0^2)$ prior on the mean: the posterior precision is $1/s_0^2 + n/\sigma^2$, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of $m_0$ and the sample mean.
:::

### The Kullback–Leibler divergence

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Kullback–Leibler divergence]{.tag} For densities $p$ and $q$ with $q > 0$ wherever $p > 0$,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \int p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\, dx .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Gibbs' inequality]{.tag} For all densities $p$ and $q$,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) \geq 0, \quad \text{with equality if and only if } p = q \text{ almost everywhere.}
$$

::: proof
By Jensen's inequality for the concave logarithm,
$$
-\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, q) = \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\log \frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\Big] \leq \log \mathbb{E}_p\Big[\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}\Big] = \log \int_{p > 0} q \leq 0 .
$$
Equality in Jensen forces $q/p$ to be constant on $\{p > 0\}$, and the second inequality forces the constant to be 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The divergence is not symmetric. Variational inference (ch. 6) minimizes $\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p)$ over an approximation $q$, and expectation propagation works with the other direction; the two give different answers.

### Markov chains

::: def
[Definition 0.9 — Markov kernel, invariance, reversibility]{.tag} A **Markov kernel** $P(x, dy)$ on a state space $E$ moves a point $x$ to a random point $y$.

A probability $\pi$ is **invariant** for $P$ if $X_0 \sim \pi$ implies $X_1 \sim \pi$, that is
$$
\int_E \pi(dx)\, P(x, dy) = \pi(dy).
$$

The kernel is **reversible** with respect to $\pi$, or satisfies **detailed balance**, if $\pi(dx) P(x, dy) = \pi(dy) P(y, dx)$ as measures on $E \times E$. Reversibility implies invariance: integrate both sides over $x$.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.10 — Ergodic theorem for Markov chains]{.tag} Let $P$ be a kernel with invariant distribution $\pi$ that is $\pi$-irreducible and Harris recurrent. Then for every $f$ integrable under $\pi$ and every starting point,
$$
\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T f(X_t) \xrightarrow[T \to \infty]{\text{a.s.}} \int f\, d\pi .
$$

The proof is in Robert and Casella (2004, ch. 6) and Meyn and Tweedie (2009).
:::

This theorem is the reason Markov chain Monte Carlo works (ch. 4 and 5): build a chain whose invariant distribution is the posterior, run it, and average along the path.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior; the evidence $p(x)$ is the normalizing constant and the hard part.
-   Gaussian conditioning (Proposition 0.2) and the linear Gaussian model (Proposition 0.3) give closed-form posteriors.
-   Exponential families have conjugate priors that act as pseudo-observations.
-   KL is non-negative and asymmetric; MCMC rests on invariance and the ergodic theorem.
:::

## 1. Decision theory {#ch1}

Learning is acting: predicting a label, choosing a dose, flagging a transaction. Decision theory compares ways of acting when the state of the world is unknown, and shows that the Bayes rule answers a precise question.

### Losses, risks and Bayes rules

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Statistical decision problem]{.tag} A **decision problem** consists of

-   a parameter space $\Theta$, the unknown state of the world, and a statistical model $P_\theta$ for the data $X$;
-   an action space $\mathcal{A}$ and a **loss function** $L : \Theta \times \mathcal{A} \to [0, \infty)$;
-   **decision rules** $\delta$, measurable maps from the data space to $\mathcal{A}$.

The (frequentist) **risk** of $\delta$ is its average loss over the data, for a fixed $\theta$:
$$
R(\theta, \delta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta\big[L(\theta, \delta(X))\big].
$$
:::

Estimation takes $\mathcal{A} = \Theta$ and, for instance, the squared loss. Testing takes $\mathcal{A} = \{0, 1\}$ and the 0–1 loss. Probabilistic prediction takes for $\mathcal{A}$ a set of distributions and the log loss, the setting of ch. 8.

The risk is a function of $\theta$, and two rules are rarely ordered for every $\theta$. There are two classical ways to summarize a risk function by a number: average it over $\theta$ (Bayes), or take its worst case (minimax).

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Bayes risk, posterior expected loss, Bayes rule]{.tag} Let $\pi$ be a prior on $\Theta$.

-   The **integrated risk** of $\delta$ is $r(\pi, \delta) = \int R(\theta, \delta)\, \pi(d\theta)$.
-   The **posterior expected loss** of an action $a$ after observing $x$ is
    $$
    \rho(\pi, a \mid x) = \mathbb{E}\big[L(\theta, a) \mid X = x\big] = \int L(\theta, a)\, \pi(d\theta \mid x).
    $$
-   A **Bayes rule** $\delta^\pi$ minimizes $r(\pi, \cdot)$ over all decision rules, and $r(\pi) = r(\pi, \delta^\pi)$ is the **Bayes risk** of $\pi$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Bayes rules minimize the posterior expected loss]{.tag} Suppose that for almost every $x$ the action $\delta^\pi(x)$ minimizes $a \mapsto \rho(\pi, a \mid x)$, and that $r(\pi, \delta^\pi) < \infty$. Then $\delta^\pi$ is a Bayes rule:
$$
r(\pi, \delta^\pi) = \min_\delta\, r(\pi, \delta).
$$

::: proof
The loss is non-negative, so Fubini's theorem lets us integrate over the joint law of $(\theta, X)$ in either order:
$$
r(\pi, \delta) = \int\!\!\int L(\theta, \delta(x))\, p(x \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, dx\, d\theta = \int \rho\big(\pi, \delta(x) \mid x\big)\, p(x)\, dx .
$$

For every rule $\delta$, the integrand is at least $\rho(\pi, \delta^\pi(x) \mid x)$ for almost every $x$. Integrating against $p(x)$ gives $r(\pi, \delta) \geq r(\pi, \delta^\pi)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key formula — the Bayes action]{.tag}
$$
\delta^\pi(x) \in \arg\min_{a \in \mathcal{A}}\; \mathbb{E}\big[L(\theta, a) \mid X = x\big]
$$
:::

The theorem is the operational content of Bayesian decision theory. There is no need to optimize over functions: after seeing $x$, minimize a function of the action. The average-over-data question and the given-the-data question have the same answer.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.4 — Bayes estimators for three standard losses]{.tag} Let $\theta$ be real with posterior $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$.

-   Squared loss $(\theta - a)^2$: the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean, and its posterior expected loss is the posterior variance.
-   Absolute loss $|\theta - a|$: any posterior median is a Bayes estimator.
-   For a discrete $\Theta$ and the 0–1 loss $\mathbb{1}\{a \neq \theta\}$: the posterior mode (MAP).

::: proof
All expectations are under the posterior.

-   Squared loss: the bias–variance decomposition
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[(\theta - a)^2] = \mathrm{Var}(\theta \mid x) + (\mathbb{E}[\theta \mid x] - a)^2
    $$
    is minimal at the posterior mean.
-   Absolute loss: let $m$ be a median and $a' > m$. The difference $|\theta - a'| - |\theta - m|$ equals $a' - m$ when $\theta \leq m$ and is at least $-(a' - m)$ otherwise. Hence
    $$
    \mathbb{E}|\theta - a'| - \mathbb{E}|\theta - m| \geq (a' - m)\big[P(\theta \leq m) - P(\theta > m)\big] \geq 0,
    $$
    because $P(\theta \leq m) \geq 1/2$. The case $a' < m$ is symmetric.
-   0–1 loss: the posterior expected loss of $a$ is $1 - \pi(a \mid x)$, minimal at the mode. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For a continuous parameter, the MAP is not a Bayes estimator for any fixed loss, and it changes under a reparameterization. It is best seen as a cheap summary of the posterior.

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — Three estimators from one posterior]{.tag} After 7 successes in 10 trials with a uniform prior, the posterior is Beta$(8, 4)$ (Example 0.6).

-   Squared loss: the posterior mean $8/12 = 0.667$.
-   Absolute loss: the posterior median $0.676$.
-   MAP: the mode $7/10 = 0.700$, which is also the maximum-likelihood estimate because the prior is flat.

Three losses encode three questions, and the same posterior gives three answers.
:::

### Admissibility and minimaxity

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Admissible and minimax rules]{.tag} A rule $\delta'$ **dominates** $\delta$ if $R(\theta, \delta') \leq R(\theta, \delta)$ for every $\theta$, with strict inequality for at least one $\theta$. A rule is **admissible** if no rule dominates it. A rule $\delta^\star$ is **minimax** if
$$
\sup_\theta R(\theta, \delta^\star) = \inf_\delta\, \sup_\theta R(\theta, \delta).
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.7 — Bayes rules are admissible]{.tag} A Bayes rule $\delta^\pi$ with $r(\pi) < \infty$ is admissible in each of the two following cases.

-   *(a)* It is the unique Bayes rule for $\pi$.
-   *(b)* $\Theta$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^d$, $\pi$ gives positive mass to every non-empty open set, and every rule has a risk continuous in $\theta$.

::: proof
Suppose that $\delta'$ dominates $\delta^\pi$.

-   *(a)* Integrating the domination against $\pi$ gives $r(\pi, \delta') \leq r(\pi, \delta^\pi)$, so $\delta'$ is also a Bayes rule. By uniqueness $\delta' = \delta^\pi$, which cannot strictly dominate itself.
-   *(b)* Let $\theta_0$ be a point of strict domination. By continuity, there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and an open neighbourhood $U$ of $\theta_0$ on which
    $$
    R(\theta, \delta') < R(\theta, \delta^\pi) - \varepsilon .
    $$
    Integrating against $\pi$, the integrated risk of $\delta'$ is at most $r(\pi) - \varepsilon\, \pi(U)$, which is smaller than the Bayes risk: a contradiction. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — A Bayes rule with constant risk is minimax]{.tag} If $R(\theta, \delta^\pi) = c$ for every $\theta$, then $\delta^\pi$ is minimax.

::: proof
For any rule $\delta$, a supremum is larger than an average, and $\delta^\pi$ minimizes the average:
$$
\sup_\theta R(\theta, \delta) \geq r(\pi, \delta) \geq r(\pi, \delta^\pi) = c = \sup_\theta R(\theta, \delta^\pi). \qquad
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.9 — A minimax estimator of a proportion]{.tag} Let $K \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, \theta)$ and take the squared loss. With a Beta$(a, a)$ prior, the Bayes estimator is $(K + a)/(n + 2a)$, and its risk is its variance plus its squared bias:
$$
R(\theta) = \frac{n\theta(1-\theta) + a^2(1 - 2\theta)^2}{(n + 2a)^2} = \frac{a^2 + (n - 4a^2)(\theta - \theta^2)}{(n + 2a)^2}.
$$

-   The risk does not depend on $\theta$ when $a = \sqrt{n}/2$. It is then
    $$
    R = \frac{1}{4(1 + \sqrt{n})^2},
    $$
    so the estimator $(K + \sqrt n/2)/(n + \sqrt n)$ is minimax by Proposition 1.8.
-   For $n = 16$ the minimax estimator is $(K + 2)/20$, with risk 0.0100 everywhere. The maximum-likelihood estimator $K/n$ has maximal risk $1/(4n) = 0.0156$, at $\theta = 1/2$.
:::

The code computes the exact risk curves of three estimators. It reports their worst-case risk and their average risk under the uniform prior:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

n = 16
theta = np.linspace(0.001, 0.999, 999)
k = np.arange(n + 1)
pmf = stats.binom.pmf(k[None, :], n, theta[:, None])     # P(K = k | theta)

def risk(est):                                             # squared-error risk R(theta, delta)
    return (pmf * (est[None, :] - theta[:, None]) ** 2).sum(axis=1)

rules = {
    "MLE k/n": k / n,
    "Bayes, uniform prior": (k + 1) / (n + 2),
    "minimax, Beta(2,2) prior": (k + 2) / (n + 4),          # a = sqrt(16)/2 = 2
}
for name, est in rules.items():
    r = risk(est)
    print(f"{name:26s} max risk {r.max():.5f}   Bayes risk (uniform) {r.mean():.5f}")
```

The maximum-likelihood estimator has worst-case risk 0.0156 and average risk 0.0104. The uniform-prior Bayes rule has the smallest average, 0.0093, as it must, and a worst case of 0.0123. The minimax rule has the smallest worst case, 0.0100, flat in $\theta$. No estimator wins for every $\theta$.

### Complete classes and Stein's paradox

::: thm
[Theorem 1.10 — Complete class theorem (Wald)]{.tag} Under regularity conditions, every admissible rule is a Bayes rule or a limit of Bayes rules. For a finite parameter space and randomized rules, every admissible rule is Bayes for some prior.

*Proof sketch for* $\Theta = \{\theta_1, \dots, \theta_k\}$. Randomized rules make the set $S$ of risk vectors $(R(\theta_1, \delta), \dots, R(\theta_k, \delta))$ convex.

An admissible rule has a risk vector $r^\star$ on the lower-left boundary of $S$. The separating hyperplane theorem gives weights $\pi_i \geq 0$ summing to 1 with $\sum_i \pi_i r^\star_i \leq \sum_i \pi_i r_i$ for every $r \in S$: the rule is Bayes for $\pi$. The general case is treated in Berger (1985) and Robert (2007).
:::

This is one precise sense in which being Bayesian helps: any sensible rule, in the sense of admissibility, is Bayes for some prior, so restricting attention to Bayes rules loses nothing. The next result shows that the most natural non-Bayesian estimator is not admissible.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.11 — James–Stein (1961)]{.tag} Let $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta, I_d)$ with $d \geq 3$, and take the loss $\|\theta - a\|^2$. The estimator
$$
\delta^{\mathrm{JS}}(X) = \Big(1 - \frac{d - 2}{\|X\|^2}\Big) X
$$
has risk
$$
R(\theta, \delta^{\mathrm{JS}}) = d - (d-2)^2\, \mathbb{E}_\theta\big[\|X\|^{-2}\big] \;<\; d = R(\theta, X),
$$
so the maximum-likelihood estimator $X$ is inadmissible when $d \geq 3$.

::: proof
*Stein's lemma*: for $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, 1)$ and a weakly differentiable $g$ with $\mathbb{E}|g'(Z)| < \infty$, an integration by parts against the Gaussian density gives $\mathbb{E}[(Z - \mu)\, g(Z)] = \mathbb{E}[g'(Z)]$.

Write $\delta^{\mathrm{JS}} = X - g(X)$ with $g(x) = (d-2)\, x / \|x\|^2$. Expanding the square,
$$
\mathbb{E}\|\delta^{\mathrm{JS}} - \theta\|^2 = d - 2\,\mathbb{E}\big[(X-\theta)^\top g(X)\big] + \mathbb{E}\|g(X)\|^2 .
$$

-   Stein's lemma, coordinate by coordinate, turns the middle expectation into $\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{div} g(X)]$, and $\operatorname{div}(x/\|x\|^2) = (d-2)/\|x\|^2$.
-   So the middle term is $-2(d-2)^2\, \mathbb{E}\|X\|^{-2}$, while the last term is $(d-2)^2\, \mathbb{E}\|X\|^{-2}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

At $\theta = 0$, $\|X\|^2$ follows a $\chi^2_d$ law with $\mathbb{E}[1/\chi^2_d] = 1/(d-2)$, so the risk drops from $d$ to 2. For $d = 10$, that is from 10 to 2. Shrinking all coordinates towards a common point helps, although they are independent: ch. 2 explains why, as empirical Bayes (Example 2.10).

### Decisions in classification and the foundations

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.12 — Cost-sensitive classification]{.tag} Labels are $y \in \{0, 1\}$ and actions $\hat y \in \{0, 1\}$. Predicting 1 when $y = 0$ costs $c_{\mathrm{FP}}$, predicting 0 when $y = 1$ costs $c_{\mathrm{FN}}$, and correct predictions cost nothing. The Bayes rule predicts 1 if and only if
$$
p(y = 1 \mid x, \mathcal{D}) > \frac{c_{\mathrm{FP}}}{c_{\mathrm{FP}} + c_{\mathrm{FN}}} .
$$

::: proof
Write $p = p(y = 1 \mid x, \mathcal{D})$. The posterior expected loss of predicting 1 is $c_{\mathrm{FP}}(1 - p)$, that of predicting 0 is $c_{\mathrm{FN}}\, p$; Theorem 1.3 picks the smaller one. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The threshold is applied to the predictive probability. If that probability is miscalibrated, the decision is wrong even with the right costs; this is why ch. 3 and ch. 8 care about predictive distributions rather than point predictions. An option to abstain at cost $c_r$ adds a third action, chosen when both expected losses exceed $c_r$.

::: note
[Foundations: expected utility]{.tag} Why maximize expected utility at all? Von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) show that preferences between lotteries satisfying completeness, transitivity, continuity and independence are represented by an expected utility. Savage (1954) goes further: preferences between acts satisfying his axioms are represented by an expected utility under a *subjective* probability, which plays the role of the prior. Parmigiani and Inoue (2009) develop these axioms and their criticisms.
:::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   The risk $R(\theta, \delta)$ averages the loss over data; the Bayes rule minimizes its average over the prior, which amounts to minimizing the posterior expected loss for the observed data (Theorem 1.3).
-   Squared, absolute and 0–1 losses give the posterior mean, median and mode.
-   Bayes rules are admissible, constant-risk Bayes rules are minimax, and admissible rules are (limits of) Bayes rules.
-   In dimension 3 or more, shrinkage beats the maximum-likelihood estimator of a Gaussian mean.
-   Cost-sensitive decisions threshold the predictive probability, so it must be calibrated.
:::

## 2. Fifty shades of Bayes: subjective and objective interpretations {#ch2}

Theorem 1.3 needs a prior. Where does it come from, and what does a posterior probability mean? Two families of answers coexist. For the **subjective** view, probability is a coherent degree of belief. For the **objective** view, the prior is a convention derived from the model. Two pragmatic positions complete the picture: estimate the prior from the data (empirical Bayes), or judge Bayesian procedures by their frequentist properties.

### Subjective Bayes: coherence and exchangeability

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Coherent previsions (de Finetti)]{.tag} An agent announces a price $P(A)$ for every event $A$ of a finite algebra. At that price she accepts to buy or sell, for any stake $s \in \mathbb{R}$, the bet that costs $s P(A)$ and pays $s\, \mathbb{1}_A$.

A **Dutch book** is a finite set of such bets whose total gain for the agent is negative in every state of the world. The prices are **coherent** if no Dutch book exists.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Coherence means probability (de Finetti, 1937)]{.tag} Prices on a finite algebra of events are coherent if and only if they form a probability: $P(A) \in [0, 1]$, $P(\Omega) = 1$, and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$ for disjoint $A$ and $B$.

::: proof
*Additivity is necessary.* Let $A, B$ be disjoint with $P(A \cup B) > P(A) + P(B)$. The opponent sells the agent a unit bet on $A \cup B$ and buys from her unit bets on $A$ and on $B$.

Since $\mathbb{1}_{A \cup B} = \mathbb{1}_A + \mathbb{1}_B$, the payoffs cancel in every state, and the agent's net gain is $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B) < 0$. Reverse the bets for the opposite inequality. The same kind of argument gives $0 \leq P(A) \leq 1$ and $P(\Omega) = 1$.

*Probability is sufficient.* If $P$ is a probability, every bet has expected gain zero under $P$, and so does every finite combination. A combination with a negative gain in every state would have a negative expectation. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Coherence gives probabilities, not a specific prior. De Finetti's second theorem explains where parameters and priors come from in the first place.

::: def
[Definition 2.3 — Exchangeability]{.tag} A sequence $(X_1, X_2, \dots)$ is **exchangeable** if, for every $n$ and every permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1, \dots, n\}$, the vectors $(X_{\sigma(1)}, \dots, X_{\sigma(n)})$ and $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ have the same law.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.4 — De Finetti's representation theorem]{.tag} An infinite exchangeable sequence of $\{0, 1\}$-valued variables is a mixture of independent Bernoulli sequences. There is a unique probability $\mu$ on $[0, 1]$ such that, with $k = x_1 + \dots + x_n$,
$$
P(X_1 = x_1, \dots, X_n = x_n) = \int_0^1 \theta^{k} (1 - \theta)^{n - k}\, \mu(d\theta),
$$
and $\mu$ is the law of the limiting frequency of ones, which exists almost surely.

::: proof
*Sketch.* Fix $N \geq n$ and let $K_N$ be the number of ones among $X_1, \dots, X_N$.

-   By exchangeability, given $K_N$, the first $n$ variables are distributed as $n$ draws *without* replacement from an urn holding $K_N$ ones and $N - K_N$ zeros.
-   As $N \to \infty$, draws without replacement approach draws with replacement, so the probability above is close to $\mathbb{E}\big[(K_N/N)^k (1 - K_N/N)^{n-k}\big]$.
-   Along a subsequence, the law of $K_N/N$ converges weakly to some $\mu$, which gives the formula. Hewitt and Savage (1955) extend the theorem to general state spaces. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The interpretation matters. If your beliefs about a sequence do not depend on the order of the observations, you behave *as if* there were a parameter $\theta$, with a prior $\mu$, and independent data given $\theta$. The parameter and the prior are consequences of a judgement on observable quantities.

### Conjugate priors as an elicitation tool

Proposition 0.5 reads a conjugate prior as pseudo-data. An expert can express a prior mean and an *equivalent sample size*, "as sure as if I had seen $m$ observations", and the two numbers fix the prior.

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Eliciting a click rate]{.tag} An expert believes a click rate is about 2 %, and is as sure as if she had seen 200 impressions. The prior is Beta$(4, 196)$.

-   After 1000 impressions with 35 clicks, the posterior is Beta$(39, 1161)$.
-   Its mean is
    $$
    39 / 1200 = 0.0325,
    $$
    between the prior mean 0.02 and the empirical rate 0.035, with weights $200/1200$ and $1000/1200$.
:::

A responsible analysis reports how the conclusions move when the prior moves within a plausible family. This *sensitivity analysis* is the subjective answer to the charge of arbitrariness.

### Objective Bayes: Jeffreys and reference priors

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — Jeffreys prior]{.tag} For a regular model with Fisher information
$$
I(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\theta\big[-\nabla^2 \log p(X \mid \theta)\big],
$$
the **Jeffreys prior** is
$$
\pi_J(\theta) \propto \sqrt{\det I(\theta)} .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Invariance under reparameterization]{.tag} Let $\varphi = h(\theta)$ with $h$ a smooth bijection. The Jeffreys prior computed in the parameter $\varphi$ is the image of $\pi_J$ under $h$.

::: proof
Let $J = \partial\theta / \partial\varphi$. By the chain rule the score transforms as $\nabla_\varphi \log p = J^\top \nabla_\theta \log p$, so the information transforms as
$$
I_\varphi(\varphi) = J^\top I_\theta(\theta)\, J, \qquad \sqrt{\det I_\varphi(\varphi)} = |\det J|\, \sqrt{\det I_\theta(\theta)} .
$$
The factor $|\det J|$ is exactly the change-of-variables factor of a density. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The point of the proposition: "ignorance" cannot be expressed by a flat prior, since a flat prior on $\theta$ is not flat on $\theta^2$. Jeffreys' rule gives the same answer whatever parameterization one starts from.

::: ex
[Example 2.8 — Jeffreys priors of common models]{.tag}

-   Bernoulli: $I(\theta) = 1/(\theta(1 - \theta))$, so $\pi_J$ is Beta$(1/2, 1/2)$.
-   Normal location with known variance: $I$ is constant, so $\pi_J$ is flat on $\mathbb{R}$.
-   Normal scale $\sigma$ with known mean: $I(\sigma) = 2/\sigma^2$, so $\pi_J(\sigma) \propto 1/\sigma$.
-   Poisson: $I(\lambda) = 1/\lambda$, so $\pi_J(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{-1/2}$.
:::

The last three priors are **improper**: they do not integrate to 1. Such a prior is acceptable only if the posterior is proper, that is if $\int p(x \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)\, d\theta$ is finite. Improper priors leave the evidence defined only up to an arbitrary constant, so they cannot be used to compare models (ch. 3).

In several dimensions the Jeffreys prior can behave badly. **Reference priors** (Bernardo, 1979; Berger, Bernardo and Sun, 2009) fix this: they maximize the expected Kullback–Leibler divergence from prior to posterior, in the limit of many replications of the experiment. In regular one-dimensional models they coincide with the Jeffreys prior.

### Empirical Bayes

::: def
[Definition 2.9 — Hierarchical model and empirical Bayes]{.tag} In a **hierarchical model**, $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_d$ are drawn independently from a prior $\pi_\lambda$ with a hyperparameter $\lambda$, and $X_i \mid \theta_i \sim p(\cdot \mid \theta_i)$. **Empirical Bayes** estimates $\lambda$ by maximizing the marginal likelihood
$$
p(x \mid \lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^d \int p(x_i \mid \theta)\, \pi_\lambda(\theta)\, d\theta ,
$$
also called type-II maximum likelihood, then uses the posterior with the estimated $\hat\lambda$. A fully Bayesian analysis puts a prior on $\lambda$ instead.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.10 — Normal means: empirical Bayes rediscovers James–Stein]{.tag} Let $\theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \tau^2)$ and $X_i \mid \theta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_i, 1)$, for $i = 1, \dots, d$.

-   Posterior mean (Example 0.6): $\mathbb{E}[\theta_i \mid X_i] = (1 - B) X_i$, with $B = 1/(1 + \tau^2)$.
-   Marginally the $X_i$ are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1/B)$, so $B\, \|X\|^2$ follows a $\chi^2_d$ law and
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{d - 2}{\|X\|^2}\Big] = B .
    $$
-   Replacing $B$ by this unbiased estimate gives exactly the James–Stein estimator of Theorem 1.11.

The coordinates are independent, but they share a hyperparameter, and each coordinate carries information on it. Efron and Morris (1973) develop this reading.
:::

### Frequentist properties of Bayesian procedures

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.11 — Bernstein–von Mises]{.tag} Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. from $p_{\theta_0}$, with $\theta_0$ interior to $\Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^d$.

Assume the model is regular (differentiable in quadratic mean, with invertible Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$), that uniformly consistent tests of $\theta_0$ exist, and that the prior has a continuous positive density at $\theta_0$. Then, in $P_{\theta_0}$-probability,
$$
\Big\| \Pi(\cdot \mid X_{1:n}) - \mathcal{N}\big(\hat\theta_n,\; \tfrac{1}{n} I(\theta_0)^{-1}\big) \Big\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \longrightarrow 0,
$$
where $\hat\theta_n$ is an efficient estimator, for instance the maximum-likelihood estimator.

::: proof
*Sketch* (van der Vaart, 1998, Theorem 10.1). Work in the local parameter $h = \sqrt{n}(\theta - \theta_0)$.

-   Local asymptotic normality: the log-likelihood ratio is $h^\top \Delta_n - \frac12 h^\top I(\theta_0) h + o_P(1)$, where $\Delta_n$ is the normalized score, asymptotically $\mathcal{N}(0, I(\theta_0))$.
-   On the scale $1/\sqrt{n}$ the prior density is nearly constant, equal to $\pi(\theta_0)$.
-   So the posterior density of $h$ is nearly proportional to $\exp(h^\top \Delta_n - \frac12 h^\top I h)$, a Gaussian with covariance $I^{-1}$. The tests control the posterior mass outside shrinking neighbourhoods of $\theta_0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Three consequences follow. In fixed dimension, the prior is forgotten at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$. A 95 % credible set is asymptotically a 95 % confidence set. And the theorem fails exactly where Bayesian methods are most interesting: in high dimension, in nonparametric models (ch. 7), and under misspecification, where the posterior concentrates at the best approximation within the model but with the wrong spread (Kleijn and van der Vaart, 2012).

The code computes the exact frequentist coverage of three 95 % intervals for a proportion with $n = 30$: the Wald interval, and the equal-tailed credible intervals under the Jeffreys and the uniform priors.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

n = 30
k = np.arange(n + 1)
z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)

def coverage(lo, hi, theta):
    inside = (lo <= theta) & (theta <= hi)
    return stats.binom.pmf(k, n, theta)[inside].sum()

phat = k / n
wald = (phat - z * np.sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n), phat + z * np.sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n))
jeff = (stats.beta.ppf(0.025, k + 0.5, n - k + 0.5), stats.beta.ppf(0.975, k + 0.5, n - k + 0.5))
unif = (stats.beta.ppf(0.025, k + 1, n - k + 1), stats.beta.ppf(0.975, k + 1, n - k + 1))

thetas = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 197)
for name, (lo, hi) in {"Wald": wald, "Jeffreys": jeff, "uniform": unif}.items():
    c = np.array([coverage(lo, hi, t) for t in thetas])
    print(f"{name:9s} mean coverage {c.mean():.3f}   min coverage {c.min():.3f}"
          f"   at theta=0.1: {coverage(lo, hi, 0.1):.3f}")
```

The Wald interval has mean coverage 0.887 and drops to 0.26 near the boundary. The Jeffreys interval has mean coverage 0.950 and minimum 0.889; the uniform-prior interval has 0.952 and 0.879. At $\theta = 0.1$ the three coverages are 0.809, 0.932 and 0.974. Brown, Cai and DasGupta (2001) recommend the Jeffreys interval on these grounds: an objective prior gives a good frequentist procedure.

### The likelihood principle

Bayesian inference depends on the data only through the likelihood function, up to a constant factor. Frequentist inference also depends on the experiments that could have happened but did not. Birnbaum (1962) showed that the sufficiency and conditionality principles together imply this **likelihood principle**.

::: ex
[Example 2.12 — Same data, two stopping rules]{.tag} A coin gives 9 heads and 3 tails. Under design A, 12 tosses were planned; under design B, the experimenter tossed until the third tail.

-   Both likelihoods are proportional to $\theta^9 (1 - \theta)^3$, so any prior gives the same posterior under both designs.
-   The one-sided p-values for $\theta = 1/2$ against $\theta > 1/2$ differ:
    $$
    p_A = 0.073 \;\;\text{(binomial)}, \qquad p_B = 0.033 \;\;\text{(negative binomial)} .
    $$

At the 5 % level, the test rejects under design B only. Lindley and Phillips (1976) discuss this example.
:::

```python
from scipy import stats
# 9 heads and 3 tails: P(at least 9 heads) under each design, for a fair coin
print("design A, binomial n = 12:        ", stats.binom.sf(8, 12, 0.5))
print("design B, stop at the third tail: ", stats.nbinom.sf(8, 3, 0.5))
```

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   Coherent betting prices are probabilities, and exchangeable beliefs behave as an i.i.d. model with a prior (de Finetti).
-   Conjugate priors encode pseudo-observations; report how conclusions move with the prior.
-   Jeffreys priors are invariant under reparameterization; improper priors need a proper posterior and cannot compare models.
-   Empirical Bayes estimates the prior from many related problems, and explains James–Stein shrinkage.
-   Bernstein–von Mises: in regular finite-dimensional models, credible sets are asymptotically confidence sets.
-   Bayesian inference obeys the likelihood principle; p-values do not.
:::

## 3. Bayesian supervised learning {#ch3}

Supervised learning the Bayesian way: put a prior on the function, through its parameters or directly, condition on the training pairs, and predict by averaging over the posterior. Linear-Gaussian models give closed forms; other models need approximations, the first of which is Laplace's.

### Bayesian linear regression

Take features $\phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^p$, the design matrix $\Phi$ with rows $\phi(x_i)^\top$, Gaussian noise of precision $\beta$ and the prior $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \alpha^{-1} I)$:
$$
y_i = w^\top \phi(x_i) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \beta^{-1}) .
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.1 — Posterior and predictive of Bayesian linear regression]{.tag} The posterior is $w \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(m_N, S_N)$ with
$$
S_N^{-1} = \alpha I + \beta\, \Phi^\top\Phi, \qquad m_N = \beta\, S_N \Phi^\top y ,
$$
and the predictive distribution at a new input $x^\star$, with $\phi^\star = \phi(x^\star)$, is
$$
y^\star \mid x^\star, y \;\sim\; \mathcal{N}\big(m_N^\top \phi^\star,\;\; \beta^{-1} + \phi^{\star\top} S_N\, \phi^\star\big).
$$
The posterior mean $m_N$ is the ridge regression estimator with penalty $\alpha / \beta$.

::: proof
Apply Proposition 0.3 with $m_0 = 0$, $S_0 = \alpha^{-1} I$ and $\Sigma = \beta^{-1} I$.

Given $y$, the new response is $y^\star = w^\top\phi^\star + \varepsilon^\star$ with $w$ and $\varepsilon^\star$ independent Gaussians, so the means and the variances add. Finally $m_N = (\Phi^\top\Phi + (\alpha/\beta) I)^{-1}\Phi^\top y$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key formula — the Bayesian linear predictive]{.tag}
$$
y^\star \mid x^\star, y \sim \mathcal{N}\big(m_N^\top \phi^\star,\; \beta^{-1} + \phi^{\star\top} S_N \phi^\star\big)
$$
:::

The predictive variance has two parts: the noise $\beta^{-1}$, which no amount of data removes (aleatoric uncertainty), and the parameter uncertainty $\phi^{\star\top} S_N \phi^\star$, which shrinks as data accumulate near $x^\star$ (epistemic uncertainty).

::: ex
[Example 3.2 — One feature, two points]{.tag} Take $\phi(x) = x$, $\alpha = 1$, $\beta = 4$ (noise standard deviation 0.5), and the data $x = (1, 2)$, $y = (1.2, 1.9)$.

-   $\sum_i x_i^2 = 5$ and $\sum_i x_i y_i = 5$, so the posterior precision is $1 + 4 \times 5 = 21$.
-   The posterior is
    $$
    w \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(20/21,\; 1/21) = \mathcal{N}(0.952,\; 0.218^2).
    $$
-   At $x^\star = 3$ the predictive mean is $2.857$ and the predictive variance $0.25 + 9/21 = 0.679$, a standard deviation of 0.824.
:::

### The marginal likelihood and model selection

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Evidence of the linear model]{.tag} Marginally $y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, C)$ with $C = \beta^{-1} I + \alpha^{-1}\Phi\Phi^\top$, so
$$
\log p(y \mid \alpha, \beta) = -\tfrac12\, y^\top C^{-1} y - \tfrac12 \log\det C - \tfrac{n}{2}\log 2\pi .
$$

::: proof
This is the marginal of Proposition 0.3. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The evidence implements **Occam's razor**. The first term rewards fit. The log-determinant penalizes models that spread their prior predictive mass over many possible data sets: since $p(y \mid \mathcal{M})$ integrates to 1 over $y$, a flexible model cannot give high density to everything.

To compare two models, Bayes' formula multiplies the prior odds by the **Bayes factor** $p(y \mid \mathcal{M}_1) / p(y \mid \mathcal{M}_2)$ (Kass and Raftery, 1995). The hyperparameters $\alpha, \beta$ can be fitted by maximizing the evidence (Definition 2.9), as MacKay (1992) proposed.

The code fits polynomials of degree 0 to 9 to 20 noisy points of $\sin(\pi x)$ and prints the training error of least squares and the log evidence:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, alpha, beta = 20, 1.0, 1 / 0.2**2          # prior precision, noise precision (sigma = 0.2)
x = np.sort(rng.uniform(-1, 1, n))
y = np.sin(np.pi * x) + 0.2 * rng.normal(size=n)

def log_evidence(Phi):
    """log p(y) for y = Phi w + noise, w ~ N(0, I/alpha), noise ~ N(0, I/beta)."""
    C = np.eye(n) / beta + Phi @ Phi.T / alpha   # marginal covariance of y
    _, logdet = np.linalg.slogdet(C)
    return -0.5 * (y @ np.linalg.solve(C, y) + logdet + n * np.log(2 * np.pi))

for deg in range(10):
    Phi = np.vander(x, deg + 1, increasing=True)
    w_ml = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi, y, rcond=None)[0]
    rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((Phi @ w_ml - y) ** 2))
    print(f"degree {deg}: training RMSE {rmse:.3f}   log evidence {log_evidence(Phi):7.2f}")
```

The training error decreases from 0.726 to 0.165. The log evidence jumps from −55.3 at degree 2 to −19.2 at degree 3, a Bayes factor of $e^{36}$, then slowly decreases to −20.3 at degree 9. The evidence picks degree 3 without any validation set, although its preference over degree 9 is weak (a factor of about 3).

A warning, known as **Lindley's paradox** (Lindley, 1957): as the prior on the extra coefficients becomes vaguer, $\alpha \to 0$, the log-determinant grows without bound and the evidence of the larger model goes to 0. Evidence-based comparisons need proper, carefully chosen priors.

### The Laplace approximation

::: def
[Definition 3.4 — Laplace approximation]{.tag} Let $\ell(\theta) = \log p(y \mid \theta) + \log p(\theta)$ have a mode $\hat\theta$ with $H = -\nabla^2 \ell(\hat\theta)$ positive definite. The **Laplace approximation** replaces the posterior and the evidence by
$$
p(\theta \mid y) \approx \mathcal{N}(\hat\theta, H^{-1}), \qquad \log p(y) \approx \ell(\hat\theta) + \frac{d}{2}\log 2\pi - \frac12 \log\det H .
$$
:::

Both come from the second-order Taylor expansion of $\ell$ at $\hat\theta$ and a Gaussian integral. For regular models with $n$ observations, the relative error on the evidence is $O(1/n)$ (Tierney and Kadane, 1986).

::: prop
[Corollary 3.5 — The Bayesian information criterion]{.tag} For $n$ i.i.d. observations, $H \approx n\, I(\hat\theta)$, so $\log\det H = d \log n + O(1)$ and
$$
\log p(y) = \log p(y \mid \hat\theta) - \frac{d}{2}\log n + O_P(1).
$$
This is the BIC of Schwarz (1978): the prior disappears into the $O_P(1)$ term.
:::

### Bayesian logistic regression

With labels $y_i \in \{0, 1\}$, $P(y_i = 1 \mid w) = \sigma(w^\top x_i)$ and the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \alpha^{-1} I)$, the posterior has no closed form. The log posterior is concave, so the MAP is found by Newton's method, and the Hessian at the mode is
$$
H = \alpha I + \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i (1 - \sigma_i)\, x_i x_i^\top, \qquad \sigma_i = \sigma(\hat w^\top x_i).
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Moderated predictions]{.tag} Under a Gaussian approximation $\mathcal{N}(m, S)$ of the posterior, the activation $a = w^\top x^\star$ is $\mathcal{N}(\mu_a, \sigma_a^2)$, with $\mu_a = m^\top x^\star$ and $\sigma_a^2 = x^{\star\top} S x^\star$.

Approximating $\sigma(a)$ by $\Phi(\lambda a)$ with $\lambda^2 = \pi/8$ gives
$$
p(y^\star = 1 \mid x^\star, \mathcal{D}) \approx \sigma\big(\kappa(\sigma_a^2)\, \mu_a\big), \qquad \kappa(s) = \big(1 + \pi s / 8\big)^{-1/2} .
$$

::: proof
Let $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ be independent of $a$. Then $\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\lambda a)] = P(Z - \lambda a \leq 0)$, and $Z - \lambda a$ is $\mathcal{N}(-\lambda\mu_a, 1 + \lambda^2\sigma_a^2)$, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\lambda a)] = \Phi\Big(\frac{\lambda\mu_a}{\sqrt{1 + \lambda^2\sigma_a^2}}\Big) \approx \sigma\Big(\frac{\mu_a}{\sqrt{1 + \lambda^2\sigma_a^2}}\Big). \qquad
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.7 — A moderated decision]{.tag} With $\mu_a = 2$ and $\sigma_a^2 = 4$, $\kappa = (1 + \pi/2)^{-1/2} = 0.624$.

-   The predictive probability is $\sigma(1.247) = 0.777$; the plug-in probability $\sigma(2)$ is 0.881.
-   With costs giving the threshold 0.8 of Proposition 1.12, the plug-in rule predicts 1 and the Bayesian rule predicts 0.

Far from the data $\sigma_a^2$ grows and the predictive probability returns towards 1/2 (MacKay, 1992).
:::

### Gaussian processes

::: def
[Definition 3.8 — Gaussian process]{.tag} A random function $f$ is a **Gaussian process** with mean $m$ and covariance kernel $k$, written $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k)$, if for all inputs $x_1, \dots, x_n$ the vector $(f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n))$ is Gaussian with
$$
\text{mean } \big(m(x_i)\big)_{i} \quad \text{and covariance} \quad K = \big[k(x_i, x_j)\big]_{i,j} .
$$
:::

Bayesian linear regression is a Gaussian process with $k(x, x') = \alpha^{-1} \phi(x)^\top \phi(x')$. Kernels with infinitely many features, such as the squared-exponential kernel, give priors on infinite-dimensional spaces of functions: a first Bayesian nonparametric model (ch. 7).

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.9 — Gaussian process regression]{.tag} Let $y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i$ with $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k)$ and independent $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. With $k_\star = (k(x_i, x^\star))_i$ and $K_\sigma = K + \sigma^2 I$, the posterior of $f(x^\star)$ is Gaussian with
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(x^\star) \mid y] = k_\star^\top K_\sigma^{-1} y, \qquad \mathrm{Var}[f(x^\star) \mid y] = k(x^\star, x^\star) - k_\star^\top K_\sigma^{-1} k_\star ,
$$
and the log marginal likelihood is
$$
\log p(y) = -\tfrac12\, y^\top K_\sigma^{-1} y - \tfrac12 \log\det K_\sigma - \tfrac{n}{2}\log 2\pi .
$$

::: proof
The vector $(f(x^\star), y)$ is Gaussian, with $\mathrm{Cov}(f(x^\star), y) = k_\star^\top$ and $\mathrm{Var}(y) = K_\sigma$. Apply Proposition 0.2. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The posterior mean is the kernel ridge regression predictor with $n\lambda = \sigma^2$, studied in [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html). The posterior variance does not depend on $y$. Exact inference costs $O(n^3)$, through a Cholesky factorization. The code fits a GP to 30 points with a gap in $(-1, 1)$ and compares length-scales by marginal likelihood:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.concatenate([rng.uniform(-3, -1, 15), rng.uniform(1, 3, 15)])
y = np.sin(2 * x) + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=x.size)
noise = 0.1**2

def k(a, b, ell):
    return np.exp(-(a[:, None] - b[None, :]) ** 2 / (2 * ell**2))

def gp(ell, xs):
    K = k(x, x, ell) + noise * np.eye(x.size)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(K)
    a = np.linalg.solve(L.T, np.linalg.solve(L, y))
    lml = -0.5 * y @ a - np.log(np.diag(L)).sum() - 0.5 * x.size * np.log(2 * np.pi)
    Ks = k(xs, x, ell)
    v = np.linalg.solve(L, Ks.T)
    sd = np.sqrt(1 - (v**2).sum(0) + noise)          # predictive sd of a new observation
    return lml, Ks @ a, sd

xs = np.array([-2.0, 0.0, 6.0])
for ell in [0.1, 0.3, 0.6, 1.0, 3.0]:
    lml, mean, sd = gp(ell, xs)
    print(f"ell={ell}: log marginal lik. {lml:7.2f}  sd at x=-2, 0, 6: {np.round(sd, 2)}")
```

The marginal likelihood is largest at $\ell = 0.6$ (8.41, against 7.24 at $\ell = 1$ and −271.6 at $\ell = 3$). With $\ell = 0.6$, the predictive standard deviation is 0.13 among the data, close to the noise level 0.1, then 0.88 in the gap and 1.00 far away, where the prior takes over. The over-smooth $\ell = 3$ gives 0.11 in the gap: confidently wrong.

Before trusting a model, check it: simulate replicated data sets from the posterior predictive and compare a statistic of interest with its observed value (Box, 1980; Gelman, Meng and Stern, 1996).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Bayesian linear regression: Gaussian posterior, ridge as its mean, predictive variance = noise + parameter uncertainty.
-   The evidence trades fit against complexity and selects models from training data, but needs proper priors.
-   Laplace: a Gaussian at the mode; BIC is its crude version. Moderation shrinks predictions towards 1/2 where the posterior is uncertain.
-   Gaussian processes: closed-form posteriors on functions, hyperparameters by marginal likelihood.
:::

## 4. Bayesian unsupervised learning {#ch4}

Unsupervised learning looks for structure that is not observed: clusters, low-dimensional factors, topics. The Bayesian version writes a generative model with latent variables and computes their posterior. Conjugacy makes the conditional distributions simple, and the Gibbs sampler exploits it.

### Mixtures and the Gibbs sampler

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Bayesian finite Gaussian mixture]{.tag} For $K$ components, $n$ observations and a known variance $\sigma^2$:
$$
w \sim \mathrm{Dir}(a_0, \dots, a_0), \qquad \mu_k \sim \mathcal{N}(0, s_0^2), \qquad z_i \mid w \sim \mathrm{Cat}(w), \qquad x_i \mid z_i, \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{z_i}, \sigma^2).
$$
The allocations $z_i$ are latent; the posterior is a distribution over $(w, \mu, z)$.
:::

The [Probabilistic Graphical Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) course fits this model by EM, which returns one maximizer of the likelihood. The Bayesian treatment keeps the whole posterior, and the simplest way to explore it is to update one block of variables at a time.

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Gibbs sampler]{.tag} For a target $\pi(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m)$ split into blocks, a systematic-scan **Gibbs sweep** replaces each block $\theta_j$ in turn by a draw from its full conditional distribution $\pi(\theta_j \mid \theta_{-j})$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — Gibbs updates preserve the target]{.tag} Each block update leaves $\pi$ invariant, and so does a full sweep.

::: proof
If $\theta \sim \pi$, the block $\theta_{-j}$ has its marginal law $\pi(\theta_{-j})$. Drawing $\theta_j' \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \theta_{-j})$ produces the pair $(\theta_j', \theta_{-j})$ with law
$$
\pi(\theta_{-j})\, \pi(\theta_j' \mid \theta_{-j}) = \pi(\theta_j', \theta_{-j}) .
$$
A composition of $\pi$-invariant kernels is $\pi$-invariant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Invariance is not enough: the chain must also be irreducible, which holds here because all conditionals have full support. The ergodic theorem (Theorem 0.10) then justifies the averages.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.4 — Full conditionals of the mixture]{.tag} With $n_k$ the number of $i$ such that $z_i = k$:

-   allocations, independently over $i$:
    $$
    p(z_i = k \mid w, \mu, x) \propto w_k\, \mathcal{N}(x_i;\, \mu_k, \sigma^2) ;
    $$
-   weights: $w \mid z \sim \mathrm{Dir}(a_0 + n_1, \dots, a_0 + n_K)$;
-   means: $\mu_k \mid z, x \sim \mathcal{N}(m_k, v_k)$, independently over $k$, with
    $$
    v_k = \Big(\frac{1}{s_0^2} + \frac{n_k}{\sigma^2}\Big)^{-1}, \qquad m_k = \frac{v_k}{\sigma^2} \sum_{i : z_i = k} x_i .
    $$

::: proof
Each full conditional is proportional to the joint density seen as a function of the block. The Dirichlet prior is conjugate to the categorical allocations, and the Gaussian prior on $\mu_k$ to the observations allocated to $k$ (Example 0.6). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The code runs this sampler on 300 points from three components with means $-4, 0, 3$ and weights $0.3, 0.5, 0.2$:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
true_mu, true_w = np.array([-4.0, 0.0, 3.0]), np.array([0.3, 0.5, 0.2])
z_true = rng.choice(3, size=300, p=true_w)
x = rng.normal(true_mu[z_true], 1.0)                 # known unit variance

K, s0, a0 = 3, 10.0, 1.0                              # mu_k ~ N(0, s0^2), w ~ Dir(a0, ..., a0)
mu, w = rng.normal(0, 1, K), np.full(K, 1 / K)
draws = []
for it in range(2000):
    # 1. allocations: p(z_i = k | ...) proportional to w_k N(x_i; mu_k, 1)
    logp = np.log(w) - 0.5 * (x[:, None] - mu[None, :]) ** 2
    p = np.exp(logp - logp.max(1, keepdims=True))
    p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    z = (p.cumsum(1) > rng.uniform(size=(x.size, 1))).argmax(1)
    n_k = np.bincount(z, minlength=K)
    # 2. weights: Dirichlet(a0 + n_k)
    w = rng.dirichlet(a0 + n_k)
    # 3. means: Gaussian, precision 1/s0^2 + n_k, mean (sum of x in k) / precision
    prec = 1 / s0**2 + n_k
    mu = rng.normal(np.bincount(z, weights=x, minlength=K) / prec, 1 / np.sqrt(prec))
    if it >= 500:
        order = np.argsort(mu)                         # relabel by sorted means
        draws.append(np.concatenate([mu[order], w[order]]))
d = np.array(draws)
print("posterior mean of (mu_1, mu_2, mu_3):", d[:, :3].mean(0).round(2))
print("posterior sd   of (mu_1, mu_2, mu_3):", d[:, :3].std(0).round(2))
print("posterior mean of (w_1, w_2, w_3):  ", d[:, 3:].mean(0).round(2))
```

The posterior means of the component means are $(-4.08, 0.02, 2.88)$, with standard deviations 0.12 to 0.16. The weights come out as $(0.25, 0.48, 0.27)$: they match the proportions actually drawn in this sample, $(0.253, 0.483, 0.263)$, rather than the generating weights.

### Label switching

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Symmetry of the mixture posterior]{.tag} If the prior is the same for every component, the posterior is invariant under every permutation of the labels. In particular, the posterior means $\mathbb{E}[\mu_k \mid x]$ are all equal.

::: proof
Permuting the labels simultaneously in $z$, $w$ and $\mu$ leaves the joint density $p(x, z, w, \mu)$ unchanged, so the posterior inherits the symmetry. Coordinates that are exchangeable under the posterior have the same marginal law, hence the same mean. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

So a sampler that explores the whole posterior gives useless component-wise averages: each average is the mean of all components. The code sorts the means at each iteration, an identifiability constraint that is harmless here because the components are well separated. In general one relabels the draws (Stephens, 2000) or reports label-free quantities: the predictive density, or the co-clustering probabilities $P(z_i = z_j \mid x)$.

The Gibbs sampler above never switches labels, because crossing between the symmetric modes requires moving many allocations at once. This is a failure to mix that happens to be convenient (Celeux, Hurn and Robert, 2000).

The number of components $K$ can be chosen by the evidence, estimated with the methods of ch. 5. Alternatively, take $K$ large with a small $a_0$: Rousseau and Mengersen (2011) show that the posterior then empties the superfluous components. Ch. 7 removes the choice altogether, with infinitely many components.

### Probabilistic and Bayesian PCA

::: def
[Definition 4.6 — Probabilistic PCA (Tipping and Bishop, 1999)]{.tag} With $W \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times q}$, $z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_q)$ and $x_i \mid z_i \sim \mathcal{N}(W z_i + \mu, \sigma^2 I_p)$, the marginal law of $x_i$ is
$$
x_i \sim \mathcal{N}\big(\mu,\; W W^\top + \sigma^2 I_p\big).
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.7 — Maximum likelihood and latent posterior]{.tag} Let $U_q$ hold the $q$ leading eigenvectors of the sample covariance and $\Lambda_q$ the matching eigenvalues. The maximum-likelihood estimates (Tipping and Bishop, 1999) are
$$
\hat W = U_q (\Lambda_q - \hat\sigma^2 I)^{1/2} R, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = \text{mean of the } p - q \text{ smallest eigenvalues},
$$
for any rotation $R$. Given $x_i$, the latent vector is Gaussian (Proposition 0.3), with $M = W^\top W + \sigma^2 I_q$:
$$
z_i \mid x_i \sim \mathcal{N}\big(M^{-1} W^\top (x_i - \mu),\; \sigma^2 M^{-1}\big).
$$
:::

**Bayesian PCA** (Bishop, 1999) puts a prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \alpha_j^{-1} I_p)$ on each column of $W$ and fits the precisions $\alpha_j$ by evidence maximization. Columns not supported by the data get $\alpha_j \to \infty$ and are switched off. This **automatic relevance determination** selects the latent dimension.

### Topic models

::: def
[Definition 4.8 — Latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei, Ng and Jordan, 2003)]{.tag} There are $K$ topics, each a distribution $\beta_k \sim \mathrm{Dir}(\eta)$ over a vocabulary of $V$ words.

Each document $d$ draws topic proportions $\theta_d \sim \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha)$. Each word position $n$ of document $d$ draws a topic $z_{dn} \sim \mathrm{Cat}(\theta_d)$, then a word $w_{dn} \sim \mathrm{Cat}(\beta_{z_{dn}})$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.9 — Collapsed Gibbs sampler for LDA (Griffiths and Steyvers, 2004)]{.tag} Integrate out $\theta$ and $\beta$.

Define three counts:

-   $n_{dk}$, the number of words of document $d$ assigned to topic $k$;
-   $n_{kv}$, the number of occurrences of word $v$ assigned to topic $k$;
-   $n_k$, the total number of words assigned to topic $k$.

A superscript $-$ means that position $dn$ is excluded from the counts. With $v = w_{dn}$,
$$
p(z_{dn} = k \mid z_{-dn}, w) \propto \big(n_{dk}^{-} + \alpha\big)\, \frac{n_{kv}^{-} + \eta}{n_{k}^{-} + V\eta} .
$$

::: proof
For a Dirichlet–multinomial pair, the marginal probability of counts $c$ is a ratio of multivariate Beta functions, $B(\alpha + c)/B(\alpha)$. Adding one count to coordinate $k$ multiplies it by $(c_k + \alpha_k)/(\sum_j c_j + \sum_j \alpha_j)$.

Apply this to the document–topic counts and to the topic–word counts. The document-side denominator does not depend on $k$ and drops out. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Latent-variable models become conditionally conjugate once the latent variables are included; the Gibbs sampler alternates their full conditionals and preserves the posterior.
-   Mixture posteriors are symmetric under relabelling: report label-free summaries or relabel.
-   Probabilistic PCA has a closed-form maximum-likelihood solution; Bayesian PCA selects the dimension by automatic relevance determination.
-   Collapsing conjugate parameters (LDA) gives samplers on discrete allocations only.
:::

## 5. Bayesian computation I: advanced Monte Carlo {#ch5}

Posterior expectations are integrals in high dimension against a density known up to a constant. Monte Carlo methods replace them by averages over samples. This chapter goes beyond the Gibbs sampler: importance sampling and its curse of dimensionality, Metropolis–Hastings, gradient-based samplers, diagnostics, and sequential Monte Carlo, which also estimates the evidence.

Throughout, the target is $\pi = \gamma / Z$, where $\gamma(\theta) = p(x \mid \theta)\, p(\theta)$ can be evaluated and $Z = p(x)$ is unknown.

### Importance sampling

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.1 — Importance sampling]{.tag} Let $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_N$ be i.i.d. from a proposal $q$ that is positive wherever $\gamma$ is, and let $w_i = \gamma(\theta_i)/q(\theta_i)$. Then
$$
\hat Z = \frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N w_i \;\text{ is unbiased for } Z, \qquad \hat I = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, f(\theta_i)}{\sum_i w_i} \xrightarrow[N \to \infty]{\text{a.s.}} \mathbb{E}_\pi[f] .
$$

::: proof
First, $\mathbb{E}_q[\gamma/q] = \int \gamma = Z$. For $\hat I$, the strong law of large numbers sends the numerator divided by $N$ to $\int f \gamma = Z\, \mathbb{E}_\pi[f]$, and the denominator divided by $N$ to $Z$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The **effective sample size** $(\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$, between 1 and $N$, measures how many draws effectively carry the estimate.

::: ex
[Example 5.2 — The curse of dimensionality]{.tag} Take the target $\mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$ and the proposal $\mathcal{N}(0, 2 I_d)$, wider than the target and centred on it.

-   In one dimension, the normalized weights satisfy $\mathbb{E}_q[w^2] = 2/\sqrt{3}$; in dimension $d$ the factors multiply.
-   The effective sample size is therefore about
    $$
    N \big(\sqrt{3}/2\big)^d ,
    $$
    that is $7.5 \times 10^{-4} N$ for $d = 50$ and $5.7 \times 10^{-7} N$ for $d = 100$.
:::

Independent proposals fail in high dimension. Markov chains move locally instead.

### Metropolis–Hastings

::: def
[Algorithm 5.3 — Metropolis–Hastings]{.tag} From the current state $\theta$, propose $\theta' \sim q(\theta, \cdot)$ and accept it with probability
$$
\alpha(\theta, \theta') = \min\Big(1,\; \frac{\gamma(\theta')\, q(\theta', \theta)}{\gamma(\theta)\, q(\theta, \theta')}\Big);
$$
otherwise stay at $\theta$. Only ratios of $\gamma$ appear, so $Z$ is never needed.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.4 — Metropolis–Hastings is reversible]{.tag} The Metropolis–Hastings kernel satisfies detailed balance with respect to $\pi$, so $\pi$ is invariant.

::: proof
For $\theta' \neq \theta$, the kernel has density $q(\theta, \theta')\, \alpha(\theta, \theta')$, and
$$
\pi(\theta)\, q(\theta, \theta')\, \alpha(\theta, \theta') = \frac{1}{Z}\min\big(\gamma(\theta)\, q(\theta, \theta'),\; \gamma(\theta')\, q(\theta', \theta)\big),
$$
which is symmetric in $(\theta, \theta')$. The rejection part is a point mass at $\theta$, symmetric on the diagonal. Definition 0.9 concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key formula — the Metropolis–Hastings ratio]{.tag}
$$
\alpha(\theta, \theta') = \min\Big(1,\; \frac{\gamma(\theta')\, q(\theta', \theta)}{\gamma(\theta)\, q(\theta, \theta')}\Big)
$$
:::

For the random-walk proposal $\theta' = \theta + h\xi$, with $\xi$ standard Gaussian, on product targets in dimension $d$, the optimal step is of order $d^{-1/2}$ and the optimal acceptance rate is 0.234 (Roberts, Gelman and Gilks, 1997). The chain then needs of order $d$ iterations to move across the target.

### Langevin and Hamiltonian samplers

The **Langevin diffusion** $d\theta_t = \frac12 \nabla \log \pi(\theta_t)\, dt + dB_t$ has $\pi$ as invariant distribution: for smooth compactly supported $f$, an integration by parts gives
$$
\int \Big(\tfrac12 \nabla\log\pi \cdot \nabla f + \tfrac12 \Delta f\Big)\, \pi \;=\; \tfrac12 \int \nabla\pi \cdot \nabla f - \tfrac12 \int \nabla \pi \cdot \nabla f = 0 .
$$
Its Euler discretization with step $h^2$ is the **unadjusted Langevin algorithm** (ULA):
$$
\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + \frac{h^2}{2} \nabla \log\gamma(\theta_k) + h\, \xi_k .
$$

ULA is biased: for a fixed step, its invariant law is not $\pi$. Using the same move as a Metropolis–Hastings proposal removes the bias: this is **MALA**. Its optimal step is of order $d^{-1/6}$, with acceptance rate 0.574 (Roberts and Rosenthal, 1998). For strongly log-concave targets, ULA has explicit non-asymptotic error bounds (Dalalyan, 2017; Durmus and Moulines, 2017). The diffusions themselves are studied in [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html).

**Hamiltonian Monte Carlo** (HMC) adds a momentum $p \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ and the energy $H(\theta, p) = -\log\gamma(\theta) + \frac12 \|p\|^2$. The Hamiltonian flow preserves $H$ and volume, so it can travel far along a level set of the joint density. It is integrated by the **leapfrog** scheme with step $\varepsilon$:
$$
p_{1/2} = p + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla\log\gamma(\theta), \qquad \theta' = \theta + \varepsilon\, p_{1/2}, \qquad p' = p_{1/2} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\nabla\log\gamma(\theta').
$$

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.5 — Properties of the leapfrog map]{.tag} Let $\Psi$ be $L$ leapfrog steps and $F(\theta, p) = (\theta, -p)$ the momentum flip. Then $\Psi$ preserves volume, and $F \circ \Psi$ is an involution: applying it twice gives the identity.

::: proof
Each of the three updates adds to one variable a function of the other, a shear with Jacobian determinant 1, so the composition preserves volume. Running the updates with the momentum reversed undoes them in reverse order, because the scheme is symmetric; hence $F \circ \Psi \circ F \circ \Psi$ is the identity. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 5.6 — Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is exact]{.tag} Draw $p \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, compute $(\theta', p') = F\circ\Psi(\theta, p)$, and accept $\theta'$ with probability $\min\big(1, e^{H(\theta, p) - H(\theta', p')}\big)$. This kernel leaves $\pi$ invariant.

*Proof sketch.* Metropolis–Hastings with a deterministic proposal that is a volume-preserving involution satisfies detailed balance, with the acceptance ratio above: the Jacobian is 1. Resampling the momentum is a Gibbs step for the joint law $\pi(\theta)\,\mathcal{N}(p; 0, I)$. Both steps preserve that law, whose $\theta$-marginal is $\pi$.
:::

The leapfrog energy error is $O(\varepsilon^2)$ over a trajectory of fixed length, so long moves are accepted with high probability; the optimal step scales as $d^{-1/4}$ (Beskos et al., 2013). The No-U-Turn sampler (Hoffman and Gelman, 2014), used by Stan, chooses the trajectory length adaptively.

The code compares the three samplers on a 50-dimensional Gaussian whose standard deviations range from 0.1 to 1, with steps tuned to the usual acceptance rates. It reports the effective sample size of the widest coordinate.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d = 50
sd = np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, d)                  # target N(0, diag(sd^2)), condition number 100
logpi = lambda x: -0.5 * np.sum((x / sd) ** 2)
grad = lambda x: -x / sd**2

def ess(chain):                                # sum autocorrelations until the first negative one
    c = chain - chain.mean()
    f = np.fft.rfft(c, 2 * c.size)
    acf = np.fft.irfft(f * np.conj(f))[:c.size] / (c.var() * c.size)
    tau = 1 + 2 * np.sum(acf[1:np.argmax(acf < 0)])
    return c.size / tau

def rwmh(h, n):
    x, out, acc = np.zeros(d), [], 0
    for _ in range(n):
        y = x + h * rng.normal(size=d)
        if np.log(rng.uniform()) < logpi(y) - logpi(x):
            x, acc = y, acc + 1
        out.append(x[-1])
    return np.array(out), acc / n

def mala(h, n):
    x, out, acc = np.zeros(d), [], 0
    logq = lambda b, a: -np.sum((b - a - 0.5 * h**2 * grad(a)) ** 2) / (2 * h**2)
    for _ in range(n):
        y = x + 0.5 * h**2 * grad(x) + h * rng.normal(size=d)
        if np.log(rng.uniform()) < logpi(y) + logq(x, y) - logpi(x) - logq(y, x):
            x, acc = y, acc + 1
        out.append(x[-1])
    return np.array(out), acc / n

def hmc(eps, L, n):
    x, out, acc = np.zeros(d), [], 0
    for _ in range(n):
        p0 = rng.normal(size=d)
        q, p = x.copy(), p0 + 0.5 * eps * grad(x)          # leapfrog integrator
        for i in range(L):
            q = q + eps * p
            p = p + (eps if i < L - 1 else 0.5 * eps) * grad(q)
        if np.log(rng.uniform()) < logpi(q) - 0.5 * p @ p - logpi(x) + 0.5 * p0 @ p0:
            x, acc = q, acc + 1
        out.append(x[-1])
    return np.array(out), acc / n

n = 10000
for name, (ch, acc), grads in [("RWMH h=0.1", rwmh(0.1, n), 0),
                               ("MALA h=0.16", mala(0.16, n), 1),
                               ("HMC eps=0.08, L=20", hmc(0.08, 20, n), 20)]:
    e = ess(ch[n // 10:])
    print(f"{name:20s} acceptance {acc:.2f}   ESS of x_50 per 1000 iterations {1000 * e / (0.9 * n):6.1f}"
          f"   gradients per iteration {grads}")
```

The acceptance rates are 0.27, 0.56 and 0.93. Per 1000 iterations, the effective sample sizes are about 1 for the random walk, 3 for MALA and 900 for HMC. Even counted per gradient evaluation, HMC gives about 45 effective draws per 1000 gradients, against 2.6 for MALA. The small scales force small steps, and only HMC turns them into long moves.

### Diagnostics

::: def
[Definition 5.7 — Autocorrelation time and effective sample size]{.tag} For a stationary chain and a function $f$ with lag-$k$ autocorrelations $\rho_k$, the **integrated autocorrelation time** and the **effective sample size** of $T$ iterations are
$$
\tau_f = 1 + 2 \sum_{k \geq 1} \rho_k, \qquad \mathrm{ESS} = T / \tau_f .
$$
Under a Markov chain central limit theorem, the variance of the ergodic average is about $\mathrm{Var}_\pi(f)\, \tau_f / T$.
:::

The $\hat R$ statistic (Gelman and Rubin, 1992; Vehtari et al., 2021) runs several chains from dispersed starting points and compares between-chain and within-chain variances; values above 1.01 signal trouble. No diagnostic proves convergence: they can only reveal its failure, as the label-switching example of ch. 4 shows.

### Sequential Monte Carlo and the evidence

::: def
[Algorithm 5.8 — Tempered sequential Monte Carlo]{.tag} Choose temperatures $0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 < \dots < \lambda_T = 1$ and the intermediate targets
$$
\gamma_t(\theta) = p(\theta)\, p(x \mid \theta)^{\lambda_t} .
$$
Start from $N$ prior draws with equal weights. For $t = 1, \dots, T$:

1.  **reweight**: multiply each weight by $p(x \mid \theta_i)^{\lambda_t - \lambda_{t-1}}$, and record the weighted mean of these factors, $\hat r_t$;
2.  **resample** the particles with probabilities proportional to their weights when the effective sample size falls below $N/2$, and reset the weights;
3.  **move** each particle with a few MCMC steps that leave $\gamma_t$ invariant, such as MALA or HMC.
:::

The product $\hat r_1 \cdots \hat r_T$ is an unbiased estimator of the evidence $Z = p(x)$, and it is consistent as $N \to \infty$ (Del Moral, Doucet and Jasra, 2006). Temperatures are usually chosen adaptively, so that each step keeps a fixed fraction of effective particles. This gives the evidence that ch. 3 and ch. 4 needed for model choice. Annealed importance sampling (Neal, 2001) is the same scheme without resampling; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos (2020) give a full treatment.

When $n$ is large, each evaluation of $\gamma$ costs $O(n)$. Bardenet, Doucet and Holmes (2017) review subsampling MCMC: naive subsampling destroys the invariant distribution, and exact methods need good control variates. Stochastic-gradient Langevin dynamics, in ch. 8, trades exactness for speed.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   Importance sampling estimates the evidence without bias but collapses in high dimension.
-   Metropolis–Hastings is reversible for any proposal; random walks need $O(d)$ steps.
-   Gradients help: MALA corrects the bias of Langevin steps, and HMC makes long, accepted moves with the leapfrog integrator.
-   Measure efficiency by effective sample size per gradient, and run several chains.
-   Tempered SMC samples the posterior and estimates the evidence.
:::

## 6. Bayesian computation II: variational methods {#ch6}

Monte Carlo is exact in the limit but can be slow. Variational inference (VI) turns inference into optimization: choose a family $\mathcal{Q}$ of tractable distributions and find its member closest to the posterior. VI scales to large data and models, at the price of a bias that this chapter makes precise.

### The evidence lower bound

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.1 — The ELBO identity]{.tag} For every density $q$ that is positive only where the posterior is,
$$
\log p(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x, \theta)] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log q(\theta)]}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(q)} \;+\; \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p(\cdot \mid x)\big).
$$

::: proof
For every $\theta$, $\log p(x) = \log p(x, \theta) - \log p(\theta \mid x)$. Take the expectation under $q$, then add and subtract $\mathbb{E}_q[\log q(\theta)]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: key
[Key formula — the evidence lower bound]{.tag}
$$
\log p(x) = \mathrm{ELBO}(q) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p(\cdot \mid x)\big) \;\geq\; \mathrm{ELBO}(q)
$$
:::

Three consequences follow. The ELBO is a lower bound on the log evidence (Proposition 0.8). Maximizing it over $q$ is the same as minimizing the divergence to the posterior. And neither requires $p(x)$.

### Mean field and coordinate ascent

The **mean-field** family contains the product densities $q(\theta) = \prod_j q_j(\theta_j)$ over blocks of variables.

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Coordinate ascent update (CAVI)]{.tag} With all factors but $q_j$ held fixed, the ELBO is maximized by
$$
q_j^\star(\theta_j) \propto \exp\Big(\mathbb{E}_{-j}\big[\log p(x, \theta)\big]\Big),
$$
where $\mathbb{E}_{-j}$ is the expectation over the other blocks under $\prod_{i \neq j} q_i$.

::: proof
As a function of $q_j$, the ELBO equals
$$
\int q_j(\theta_j)\, \mathbb{E}_{-j}[\log p(x, \theta)]\, d\theta_j - \int q_j \log q_j + \text{const} = -\mathrm{KL}(q_j \,\|\, q_j^\star) + \text{const},
$$
since $\log q_j^\star = \mathbb{E}_{-j}[\log p(x, \theta)]$ minus a constant. By Proposition 0.8 the maximum is reached at $q_j = q_j^\star$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Cycling through the blocks never decreases the ELBO, and converges to a local optimum. The update has the same shape as a Gibbs conditional, with random neighbours replaced by expectations.

::: ex
[Example 6.3 — Mean field on a Gaussian]{.tag} Take the target $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Lambda^{-1})$ in two dimensions, a stand-in for a posterior. As a function of $\theta_1$, the expected log density is quadratic with coefficient $-\frac12\Lambda_{11}$, so CAVI gives
$$
q_1 = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_1 - \Lambda_{11}^{-1}\Lambda_{12}(m_2 - \mu_2),\; \Lambda_{11}^{-1}\big),
$$
